scenario.title: The new bank details
scenario.type: Business email compromise and payment fraud

band.label: Developing
band.text: Core decisions were right, with gaps in timing, communication or a few calls to revisit.

log.title: The payment that never arrived
log.choice: Wait for the internal investigation to confirm fraud before involving the bank.
log.consequence: The investigation confirms fraud at 15:00. By then the receiving bank has processed two outgoing transfers.

log.title: Whose mailbox?
log.choice: Treat the clerk's mailbox as compromised: revoke sessions, reset the password, remove the rule and any MFA method or app consent the attacker added, then hunt the tenant for the same rule pattern and sign-ins. Warn Contoso by phone that their mailbox is compromised.
log.consequence: Two more mailboxes with the same rule are found in Finance and cleaned. Contoso's IT starts its own response after your call.

log.title: How they got in
log.consequence: No decision was recorded in time; legacy authentication stays open across the tenant.

log.title: What did they read?
log.choice: Preserve and review available mailbox audit and synchronisation records, document when the breach became known, and have Legal and the DPO assess personal-data exposure, evidence limitations and each applicable notification threshold and deadline.
log.consequence: The audit log shows the attacker synchronised the whole mailbox. The DPO assesses a risk to individuals and schedules the regulator notice within the deadline.

log.title: Who owes what?
log.choice: Notify the insurer under the crime and social-engineering cover, review the contract's payment-change clauses with counsel, and answer Contoso in writing without admitting liability, proposing a joint review of their compromised mailbox.
log.consequence: The insurer accepts the claim under the social-engineering sub-limit. Contoso agrees to a joint review, and deliveries continue.

log.title: Your mailbox, their fraud
log.choice: Publish a generic fraud warning on the website.
log.consequence: Few customers see it; a second customer pays CAD 40,000 to the attacker the next day.

log.title: Never again
log.choice: Call back on a known number for any bank-detail change, dual approval for changes to the ERP supplier master, alerts on master-data changes and new payees, legacy authentication blocked, and inbox-rule detection in the SOC.
log.consequence: The board approves the package. The first alert fires a month later on a real change request, and the call-back works.

actions.action: In payment fraud the first hours decide what can be recovered; call the bank on suspicion.
No decision was made in time: Close the access path the attacker used for every account that shares it, then verify with sign-in monitoring.
Add All staff to the notification list for this decision.
Add Cyber insurer to the notification list for this decision.
Warn the people who were actually targeted, directly.

hotwash: How long did it take from the supplier's call to the bank's recall request?
Which channel did we use to verify facts, and could the attacker read it?
Who knew that legacy authentication was still allowed, and why was it?
Which customers were told directly, and who decided?
What single control would have stopped this payment?
